input.contents: import { Block, Bold, Code, CodeBlock, Italic, List, ListItem, renderToMarkdown, Span, Title } from '../../lib/markdown'; import type { InternalSkill } from './types'; export const pdfSkill: InternalSkill = { name: 'pdf-handling', description: 'How to get data out of a PDF, and what to do when the usual read does not work: scanned files with no text layer, tables whose layout is lost, and figures that need reading as an image. Load this before working with a .pdf file.', body: renderToMarkdown( Working with PDFs Reading a PDF with read gives you its text layer, page by page, prefixed with a{' '} --- Page N --- marker and a header saying how many pages the file has. Start there. The rest of this skill is about the cases where that is not enough. Trust the page count The header tells you the true number of pages; the body may be cut short because a long read is truncated. If the last marker you can see is well below the page count, you have not read the whole document. Say so rather than answering as if you had, and read again with a narrower goal or work through a sandbox. A PDF with no text layer A scanned document — a photographed invoice, a signed contract, an old report — has no text layer, and{' '} read fails saying so. It is not a corrupt file and re-reading will not help. Two ways forward, in order of preference: If the user also attached the page as an image, read the image instead: you can see images directly, and that is the fastest route for one or two pages. Otherwise tell the user plainly that the PDF is scanned and its text cannot be extracted, and ask whether they can supply the underlying data (a CSV, an export, the original spreadsheet). Offer OCR only if a sandbox is available, and warn that OCR on a table is unreliable. Never guess at the contents of a scanned PDF from its filename. Tables and layout PDF has no concept of a table: what looks like a grid is absolutely-positioned text, and extraction flattens it into lines. Numbers may end up separated from their labels, columns may interleave, and a figure like 1,234 may arrive split. So: read a PDF to understand a document, quote from it, or find where something is stated. Do not treat extracted rows as data to compute with. If a user wants totals, growth, or any figure you would have to recompute, either take the numbers the document itself states, and say which page they came from, or ask for the data behind the report, or parse it properly in a sandbox (below). Never silently transcribe a PDF table into a chart or a SQL insert. A transcription error in a financial table is the kind of mistake that destroys trust in every other number you produce. Parsing properly in a sandbox When execute_sandboxed_code is available and the document really has to be parsed, mount the file with storage_files and use a library built for the job: {`storage_files: ["/home/uploads/2026-01-31/report.pdf"] packages: ["pdfplumber"]`} {`import pdfplumber with pdfplumber.open("files/uploads/2026-01-31/report.pdf") as pdf: page = pdf.pages[3] for table in page.extract_tables(): for row in table: print(row)`} pdfplumber keeps column structure far better than a plain text extract, which is the whole reason to bother with a sandbox. Print what you found and check it looks like a table before you use it. For a scanned file you would need OCR instead (pytesseract plus the{' '} tesseract-ocr system package), which is slow and often wrong on numbers — get the user's agreement first. Reporting back Cite pages when you quote or attribute a figure ("page 4 gives Q3 revenue as €1.2M"). It is what makes an answer from a document checkable, and the user has the file open in front of them. , ), };

input.explanation: This is an architectural design question with multiple approaches and trade-offs (sidecar text files, on-the-fly extraction, cache). Plan mode fits better than jumping to an implementation.

questions.prompt: grep today runs ripgrep on raw file bytes, so it cannot usefully search a .pdf (binary). Which direction do you want?

options.label: On first successful read (or upload), write a text sidecar next to the PDF (e.g. report.pdf.txt) that ripgrep can search; show matches against the virtual .pdf path
Special-case grep for .pdf paths: extract text with extractPdfText (same as read), then run the pattern in-process — no sidecar on disk
No tool change — teach the pdf skill to write extracted text via sandbox/write, then grep that text file
Not sure yet — sketch the trade-offs first, then pick

content.text:
Today `read` runs `extractPdfText` on PDFs, but `grep` only runs ripgrep on raw bytes — so binary PDFs are effectively unsearchable (and on S3, `/home` grep is off entirely).

A few ways to close that gap; they diverge a lot:

1. **Sidecar on extract** — On first successful `read` (or upload) of a PDF with a text layer, write something like `report.pdf.txt` (or a hidden `.nao/extracted/...` twin) with the same text `read` returns. Grep keeps using ripgrep; matches can be remapped to the `.pdf` path. Cheap after the first extract; works with directory greps; needs invalidation if the PDF is replaced; still local-fs only unless you also change S3 grep.

2. **Inline extract in grep** — If the target is a `.pdf` (or a walk finds ones), call `extractPdfText` and match the pattern in-process (or write a temp file for rg). No extra files; always fresh; slower on big trees (extract every PDF); awkward for “grep the whole `/home`” unless you cap which files get extracted.

3. **Skill / agent workflow only** — Teach the pdf skill: extract once (sandbox or `read` + `write`), save text under `/home`, then `grep` that. No tool changes; relies on the model doing the right thing; doesn’t help until something has been parsed.

“When applicable” fits **(1) or (2)** for PDFs that already have a text layer (same cases `read` succeeds; scanned PDFs stay “no text”).

Which do you want to pursue? My default if you don’t care: **sidecar written on first successful extract**, remapped so the agent still sees `/home/.../file.pdf` in grep hits — best fit for “grep the uploads folder” without re-parsing every time.
